source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XI (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio primi capituli: Initium Evangelii Jesu Christi Filii Dei
1.title_en: Exposition of the first chapter: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God

paras.t: Præmittit sanctus Evangelista operi suo prologum quemdam brevissimum, qui finitur ibi: Fuit Joannes in deserto baptizans. Ibi enim inchoatur narratio. Ait ergo: Initium Evangelii, id est exordium bonæ annuntiationis, in qua annuntiatur salus æterna, et promittitur regnum cœleste, id est evangelicæ legis et christianæ doctrinæ, Jesu Christi Filii Dei, id est tractantis de Jesu Christo, imo et dati ab eo qui est Filius Dei, non adoptivus, sed naturalis. Christus enim est primus et principalis magister evangelicæ veritatis, et de ipso tractat Evangelium ab Evangelistis conscriptum. Itaque, Initium hujus Evangelii, hoc est id a quo ego Evangelii descriptionem incipio, est sicut scriptum est, id est, id quod scriptum est, in Isaia propheta. Sicut enim, interdum significat similitudinem, et interdum denotat veritatem, ut hoc loco.
paras.en: The holy Evangelist puts before his work a very short prologue, which ends at the words: [[1:4|John was in the desert, baptizing|Fuit Joannes in deserto baptizans]]. For there the narrative begins. He says, then: [[1:1|The beginning of the gospel|Initium Evangelii]], that is, the opening of the good tidings, in which eternal salvation is announced and the heavenly kingdom promised, that is, of the law of the Gospel and of Christian teaching, [[1:1|of Jesus Christ, the Son of God|Jesu Christi Filii Dei]], that is, the Gospel that treats of Jesus Christ, and indeed was given by him who is the Son of God, not adoptive but natural. For Christ is the first and principal master of the truth of the Gospel, and the Gospel written by the Evangelists treats of him. So, the beginning of this Gospel, that is, that from which I begin my writing of the Gospel, [[1:2|As it is written|est sicut scriptum est]], that is, is what is written, [[1:2|in Isaias the prophet|in Isaia propheta]]. For 'as' sometimes signifies likeness and sometimes denotes the truth, as in this place.

paras.t: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, hoc est Joannem præcursorem, qui angelus, id est nuntius, appellatur, et propter sui officii dignitatem, vitæ perfectionem et contemplationis altitudinem, merito angelus dictus est, non quod superioris esset naturæ seu angelus incarnatus, ut dixerunt hæretici; ante faciem tuam, id est ante te, et ante tuam declarationem seu tuæ præsentiæ manifestationem, o Christe, videlicet, ut te annuntiet et ostendat hominibus. Hæc enim verba allegantur hoc loco in persona Dei ad Christum loquentis. Qui præparabit viam tuam, hoc est, actus bonos seu opera virtuosa dispositive inducet in cordibus Judæorum, per quæ intras corda hominum. Per talia enim disponuntur mentes humanæ ad Christi receptionem, qui secundum Apostolum, per fidem habitat in cordibus nostris. Ante te, hoc est, antequam ingrediaris corda humana; vel, Ante te, id est in conspectu tuo, et coram te, teque præsente. Per hoc enim quod Joannes Baptista docendo, baptizando, monstrando ac protestando disposuit populum Judæorum ad Christi notitiam, præparavit Christo ingressum ad animas Judæorum. Denique doctrina atque baptismus Joannis, fuerunt quædam præparationes doctrinæ et Baptismatis Christi, quoniam per baptismum et doctrinam Joannis disponebantur Judæi ad recipiendum doctrinam et Baptismum Domini Salvatoris. Potest ergo et ita exponi: Qui præparabit viam tuam ante te, id est, ad tuæ doctrinæ ac Baptismi receptionem disponet suos auditores. Vox clamantis in deserto: Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas ejus. Hoc totum in Matthæo diligenter et prolixe expositum est.
paras.en: [[1:2|Behold I send my angel|Ecce ego mitto angelum meum]], that is, John the Forerunner, who is called an angel, that is, a messenger, and is rightly called an angel because of the dignity of his office, the perfection of his life and the height of his contemplation; not because he was of a higher nature, or an angel incarnate, as heretics have said. [[1:2|before thy face|ante faciem tuam]], that is, before you, and before your declaration, or the manifestation of your presence, O Christ: namely, to announce you and show you to men. For these words are cited here in the person of God speaking to Christ. [[1:2|who shall prepare the way|Qui præparabit viam tuam]], that is, will bring about in the hearts of the Jews, by way of disposing them, good acts or virtuous works, through which you enter the hearts of men. For by such things human minds are disposed to receive Christ, who, according to the Apostle, dwells by faith in our hearts[[Eph 3:17||]]. [[1:2|before thee|Ante te]], that is, before you enter human hearts; or, before you, that is, in your sight and before you, in your presence. For by disposing the Jewish people to the knowledge of Christ by teaching, baptizing, pointing out and testifying, John the Baptist prepared Christ's entry into the souls of the Jews. Lastly, John's teaching and baptism were certain preparations for Christ's teaching and Baptism, since by John's baptism and teaching the Jews were disposed to receive the teaching and Baptism of the Lord our Saviour. It can therefore also be expounded thus: [[1:2|who shall prepare the way before thee|Qui præparabit viam tuam ante te]], that is, will dispose his hearers to receive your teaching and Baptism. [[1:3|A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord; make straight his paths|Vox clamantis in deserto: Parate viam Domini, rectas facite semitas ejus]]. All this has been carefully and at length expounded in Matthew[[Matt 3:3||]].

paras.t: Sed quæstio oritur, quomodo Marcus dicat hoc testimonium in Isaia descriptum, quum prima pars ejus scripta sit in Malachia, et altera in Isaia. Ad hoc doctores catholici diversimode respondent. Hieronymus enim putat nomen Isaiæ scriptorum vitio additum. Alii dicunt, quod Marcus brevitati studens, nomen Malachiæ omisit, eo quod ultima pars hujus prophetiæ habeatur in Isaia, et quoniam Isaias principalior fuit, res autem a fine et a principaliori nomen sortitur. Sed vere et indubitanter dici potest, quod tota jam allegata auctoritas in Isaia habetur quantum ad sensum, licet quoad tenorem verborum prima pars ejus in solo Malachia contineatur. Unde Marcus in lege et Prophetis etiam humano studio ante suam conversionem eruditus, nomen et verba Isaiæ commemorans, verba Malachiæ interserit tanquam declarativa verborum Isaiæ. Quis enim est angelus Dei ante Christum missus, et viam ejus adventui præparans, nisi Joannes, vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Domini?
paras.en: But a question arises: how does Mark say that this testimony is written in Isaias, when its first part is written in Malachias[[Mal 3:1||]] and the other in Isaias[[Is 40:3||]]? To this the Catholic doctors answer in different ways. For Jerome thinks the name of Isaias was added by a fault of the scribes. Others say that Mark, aiming at brevity, left out the name of Malachias, because the last part of this prophecy is found in Isaias, and since Isaias was the more principal, and a thing takes its name from its end and from the more principal part. But it can be said truly and without doubt that the whole text cited is found in Isaias as to its sense, though as to the wording its first part is contained in Malachias alone. So Mark, who before his conversion had been learned in the law and the Prophets by human study as well, in recalling the name and words of Isaias puts in the words of Malachias as explaining the words of Isaias. For who is the angel of God sent before Christ and preparing the way for his coming, if not John, [[Is 40:3|The voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord|vox clamantis in deserto, Parate viam Domini]]?

paras.t: Insuper quæritur, cur Marcus ita allegat, Ecce mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam, etc., quum in Malachia sic scriptum sit, Ecce mitto angelum meum et præparabit viam ante faciem meam? Dicendum, quod Christus et Apostoli atque Evangelistæ frequenter allegant Scripturas veteris Testamenti potius quoad sensum quam formam verborum. Sic nunc efficit Marcus. Nec discrepat quod Marcus allegat, a prædictis verbis Malachiæ, sed omnino redit in idem, quia per faciem Dei Patris uno modo intelligitur Christus. Nam sicut per faciem res ipsa cognoscitur ac monstratur, sic per Filium cognoscitur et ostenditur Pater; item, quia ad quemcumque venit Filius, venit et Pater, sicque Joannes parando viam Christo, paravit viam et Patri.
paras.en: It is asked besides why Mark cites it so, [[1:2|Behold I send my angel before thy face|Ecce mitto angelum meum ante faciem tuam]], etc., when in Malachias it is written thus: [[Mal 3:1|Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face|Ecce mitto angelum meum et præparabit viam ante faciem meam?]]. It must be said that Christ and the Apostles and Evangelists often cite the Scriptures of the Old Testament according to the sense rather than the form of the words. So Mark does now. Nor does what Mark cites differ from the said words of Malachias; it comes to exactly the same, since in one way Christ is understood by the face of God the Father. For as a thing is known and shown by its face, so the Father is known and shown by the Son; also, to whomever the Son comes the Father comes too, and so John, in preparing the way for Christ, prepared the way for the Father as well.

paras.t: Fuit Joannes in deserto Judææ trans Jordanem, baptizans. Sicut enim nascendo et prædicando, Christi nativitatem et prædicationem prævenit, sic et baptizando, Christi Baptismum prævenit, servans ubique suæ ordinem præcursionis. Et prædicans baptismum pœnitentiæ, id est Baptismum Christi ordinatum ad agendam pœnitentiam: Baptismum, inquam, valentem in remissionem peccatorum, quia per Christi Baptismum diluuntur peccata. Prædicavit autem Joannes Baptismum Christi cito futurum, quum dixit: Ego vos baptizo in aqua; ille vos baptizabit in Spiritu Sancto et igni. Verumtamen ipse Jesus non baptizavit generaliter, sed discipuli ejus. De hac materia multa tractata sunt supra in Matthæo: idcirco prætermitto.
paras.en: [[1:4|John was in the desert|Fuit Joannes in deserto]] of Judea beyond the Jordan, [[1:4|baptizing|baptizans]]. For as by his birth and preaching he went before Christ's birth and preaching, so by baptizing he went before Christ's Baptism, everywhere keeping the order of his forerunning. [[1:4|and preaching the baptism of penance|Et prædicans baptismum pœnitentiæ]], that is, the Baptism of Christ ordered to doing penance: a Baptism, I say, availing [[1:4|unto remission of sins|in remissionem peccatorum]], since sins are washed away by the Baptism of Christ. John preached the Baptism of Christ soon to come when he said: [[Matt 3:11|I indeed baptize you in water|Ego vos baptizo in aqua]]; [[Matt 3:11|he shall baptize you in the Holy Ghost and fire|ille vos baptizabit in Spiritu Sancto et igni]]. Yet [[John 4:2|Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples|ipse Jesus non baptizavit generaliter, sed discipuli ejus]], not generally. Much has been treated of this matter above in Matthew; so I pass it over.

paras.t: Et egrediebatur ad illum, videlicet ad Joannem tunc exsistentem circa Jordanem: venit enim a deserti latibulis ad ripam Jordanis, ut populum baptizaret; omnis Judææ regio, id est omnes habitantes in regione Judæorum, hoc est quidam de omnibus, et Jerosolymitæ universi, id est habitatores Jerusalem. Ista distributio intelligenda est pro generibus singulorum, non pro singulis generum, ut sit hyperbolica locutio. Juxta quem modum ait Apostolus: Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt, non quæ Jesu Christi. Et baptizabantur ab illo in Jordane flumine, confitentes peccata sua in generali, non confessione sacramentali, prout Confessio ponitur novæ legis sacramentum.
paras.en: [[1:5|And there went out to him|Et egrediebatur ad illum]], namely to John, who was then about the Jordan: for he came from the hiding places of the desert to the bank of the Jordan to baptize the people[[Luke 3:3||]]; [[1:5|all the country of Judea|omnis Judææ regio]], that is, all who lived in the region of the Jews, that is, some of all, [[1:5|and all they of Jerusalem|et Jerosolymitæ universi]], that is, the inhabitants of Jerusalem. This distribution is to be understood over the kinds of individuals, not over the individuals of each kind, so that it is a hyperbolical expression; in which manner the Apostle says: [[Phil 2:21|all seek the things that are their own not the things that are Jesus Christ's|Omnes quæ sua sunt quærunt, non quæ Jesu Christi]]. [[1:5|and were baptized by him in the river of Jordan, confessing their sins|Et baptizabantur ab illo in Jordane flumine, confitentes peccata sua]] in general, not by sacramental confession, in the sense in which Confession is set down as a sacrament of the new law.

paras.t: Et erat Joannes vestitus pilis cameli. Quod hic de vestitu et victu Joannis inducitur, scriptum atque expositum est in Matthæo. Et prædicabat dicens: Venit fortior me post me, utpote Christus, virtus et sapientia Patris: de quo ait Psalmista: Dominus virtutum ipse est rex gloriæ. Hic venit post Joannem, quoniam sicut natus est de Virgine post Joannem, sic etiam cœpit se manifestare, docere et miracula facere, post inchoationem prædicationis Joannis. Cujus non sum dignus procumbens, id est, ante eum inclinans seu procidens, solvere corrigiam calceamentorum ejus, id est in re corporali, exteriori et minima ei servire, propter incomparabilem ejus excellentiam super me. Omnia ista plenius elucidata sunt in Matthæo. Ego baptizavi vos aqua, corpora abluendo, non animas a vitiis expurgando, quia baptismus meus non confert nec continet gratiam; ille vero baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto, id est in suo Baptismo gratiam Spiritus Sancti intus purgantem vobis infundet, dummodo volueritis credere in eum: ficte enim accedentibus non infunditur gratia. In Baptismo imprimitur tamen character: propter quod non rebaptizabantur, quoniam fictione cessante, Baptismus consequitur suum effectum.
paras.en: [[1:6|And John was clothed camel's hair|Et erat Joannes vestitus pilis cameli]]. What is brought in here about John's clothing and food has been written and expounded in Matthew[[Matt 3:4||]]. [[1:7|And he preached, saying: There cometh after me one mightier than I|Et prædicabat dicens: Venit fortior me post me]], namely Christ, [[1 Cor 1:24|the power of God and the wisdom of God|virtus et sapientia]] the Father's: of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 23:10|the Lord of hosts, he is the King of Glory|Dominus virtutum ipse est rex gloriæ]]. He comes after John, since as he was born of the Virgin after John, so too he began to show himself, to teach and to work miracles after John's preaching had begun. [[1:7|the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and loose|cujus non sum dignus procumbens solvere corrigiam calceamentorum ejus]]: 'to stoop down', that is, bowing or falling down before him; that is, to serve him in a bodily, outward and very small thing, because of his incomparable excellence over me. All this has been more fully explained in Matthew[[Matt 3:11||]]. [[1:8|I have baptized you with water|Ego baptizavi vos aqua]], washing bodies, not cleansing souls from vices, since my baptism neither confers nor contains grace; [[1:8|but he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost|ille vero baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto]], that is, in his Baptism he will pour into you the grace of the Holy Ghost that cleanses within, provided you are willing to believe in him: for grace is not poured into those who come insincerely. Yet in Baptism a character [the indelible mark of the sacrament] is imprinted; for which reason they were not rebaptized, since when the insincerity ceases, Baptism obtains its effect.

paras.t: Et factum est in diebus illis, venit Jesus a Nazareth Galilææ ad Joannem, et baptizatus est in Jordane a Joanne: non quia indiguit, sed ut omnem impleret justitiam, ut humilitatis daret exemplum, ut aquis vim regenerativam præstaret, et Joannis baptismum confirmaret, nobisque maximam gratiam mereretur. Et confestim ascendens de aqua Jordanis, vidit cœlos apertos, et Spiritum tanquam columbam descendentem et manentem in ipso. Hoc tam de Christo quam de Joanne intelligi potest: uterque enim simul exivit de aqua Jordanis; tuncque ambo viderunt cœlos apertos, et Spiritum Sanctum in forma columbæ super caput Christi descendere atque manere. Et vox de cœlo facta est, id est ab angelo loquente in persona Dei Patris in aere seu cœlo aerio. Tu, Christe, es Filius meus dilectus, in te complacui. De hac superbenedictæ Trinitatis apparitione in Christi baptismo, et quo modo intelligenda sit cœlorum apertio, aliisque notabilibus præsentem concernentibus locum, introducta sunt plurima in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[1:9|And it came to pass, in those days, Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee|Et factum est in diebus illis, venit Jesus a Nazareth Galilææ]] to John, [[1:9|and was baptized by John in Jordan|et baptizatus est in Jordane a Joanne]]: not because he needed it, but [[Matt 3:15|to fulfil all justice|ut omnem impleret justitiam]], to give an example of humility, to give the waters regenerating power, to confirm John's baptism, and to merit for us the greatest grace. [[1:10|And forthwith coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens open and the Spirit as a dove descending and remaining on him|Et confestim ascendens de aqua Jordanis, vidit cœlos apertos, et Spiritum tanquam columbam descendentem et manentem in ipso]]. This can be understood both of Christ and of John: for both came up together out of the water of the Jordan, and then both saw the heavens opened and the Holy Ghost in the form of a dove descending and remaining upon Christ's head. [[1:11|And there came a voice from heaven|Et vox de cœlo facta est]], that is, from an angel speaking in the person of God the Father in the air, or the heaven of the air: [[1:11|Thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased|Tu, Christe, es Filius meus dilectus, in te complacui]], O Christ. Of this appearance of the most blessed Trinity at Christ's baptism, of how the opening of the heavens is to be understood, and of other notable things concerning the present place, a great deal was brought in on Matthew[[Matt 3:16||]].

paras.t: Et statim post receptionem baptismi, Spiritus sanctus expulit, id est, prompte ac fervide movit et duxit eum, scilicet Christum, in desertum. Christus namque, secundum assumptam humanitatem, in omnibus promptissime atque celerrime obedivit instinctui Spiritus Sancti, tanquam plenissimus septem donis Spiritus Sancti, per quæ redditur anima bene mobilis a Spiritu Sancto, juxta illud Apostoli: Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei. Et ad hoc insinuandum, Evangelista ait: Expulit eum. Et erat in deserto quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus; et tentabatur a Satana. Hoc totum in Matthæo expositum est. Eratque cum bestiis eremi, quæ ei nocere non poterant; et angeli ministrabant ei, tanquam superiori ac Domino majestatis: sicque rationalia et irrationalia ei subjecta fuerunt. Per quod ostenditur duplex in Christo natura, puta humana, ac divina. Quod enim cum bestiis versabatur, humanæ naturæ fuit humilitas; quod vero ab angelis honorabatur, divinæ exstitit majestatis indicium.
paras.en: [[1:12|And immediately|Et statim]], after receiving baptism, [[1:12|the Spirit drove him out|Spiritus sanctus expulit]], that is, moved and led him promptly and fervently, namely Christ, [[1:12|into the desert|in desertum]]. For Christ, according to the humanity he assumed, obeyed the prompting of the Holy Ghost in all things most promptly and swiftly, as being most full of the seven gifts of the Holy Ghost, by which the soul is made readily movable by the Holy Ghost, according to the Apostle's words: [[Rom 8:14|whosoever are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God|Quicumque Spiritu Dei aguntur, hi sunt filii Dei]]. And to suggest this the Evangelist says: drove him out. [[1:13|And he was in the desert forty days and forty nights, and was tempted by Satan|Et erat in deserto quadraginta diebus et quadraginta noctibus; et tentabatur a Satana]]. All this has been expounded in Matthew[[Matt 4:2||]]. [[1:13|And he was with beasts|Eratque cum bestiis]] of the wilderness, which could not harm him; [[1:13|and the angels ministered to him|et angeli ministrabant ei]], as to their superior and the Lord of majesty: and so rational and irrational things were subject to him. By this the twofold nature in Christ is shown, human and divine. For his living among the beasts was the lowliness of human nature, while his being honoured by the angels was a sign of divine majesty.

paras.t: Postquam autem traditus est Joannes, id est ab Herode captus et incarceratus, venit Jesus in Galilæam, prædicans generaliter et publice, Evangelium regni Dei, id est doctrinam novæ legis, in qua annuntiatur regnum cœleste, quæ etiam sua observatione introducit ad illud. Sciendum quod ante incarcerationem Joannis, Christus collegit quosdam discipulos, prædicavit, et quædam miracula fecit, prout Joannes evangelista testatur. Tamen, quoniam prædicatio Joannis præparatoria fuit ad Christi prædicationem, propterea non prædicavit publice et communiter, nisi post traditionem Joannis. Ideo Marcus loquitur ac si Christus prædicationem suam incepisset post comprehensionem Præcursoris. Et dicens: Quoniam impletum est tempus: hoc est, plenitudo temporis jam advenit in quo Pater me misit Filium suum, et tempus gratiæ a Prophetis prænuntiatum nunc adest. Unde in Actibus ait Petrus: Omnes Prophetæ a Samuel et deinceps, annuntiaverunt dies istos. Et appropinquabit regnum Dei, id est, janua regni cœlestis per meam passionem cito aperietur, et sempiterna hæreditas tribuetur electis. Pœnitemini, id est, de peccatis vestris compungimini et dolete, et credite Evangelio, id est evangelicæ prædicationi ac legi quam vobis propono.
paras.en: [[1:14|And after that John was delivered up|Postquam autem traditus est Joannes]], that is, taken and imprisoned by Herod, [[1:14|Jesus came in Galilee, preaching|venit Jesus in Galilæam, prædicans]] generally and publicly [[1:14|the gospel of the kingdom of God|Evangelium regni Dei]], that is, the teaching of the new law, in which the heavenly kingdom is announced, and which by being kept also leads into it. It should be known that before John's imprisonment Christ gathered some disciples, preached, and worked some miracles, as John the evangelist testifies[[John 1:37||]][[John 3:24||]]. Yet since John's preaching was preparatory to Christ's preaching, he did not preach publicly and commonly until after John was delivered up. So Mark speaks as if Christ had begun his preaching after the Forerunner's arrest. [[1:15|And saying: The time is accomplished|Et dicens: Quoniam impletum est tempus]]: that is, [[Gal 4:4|the fulness of the time was come|plenitudo temporis jam advenit]] in which the Father has sent me, his Son, and the time of grace foretold by the Prophets is now here. Hence Peter says in the Acts: [[Acts 3:24|all the prophets, from Samuel and afterwards|Omnes Prophetæ a Samuel et deinceps]], [[Acts 3:24|have told of these days|annuntiaverunt dies istos]]. [[1:15|and the kingdom of God is at hand|Et appropinquabit regnum Dei]], that is, the gate of the heavenly kingdom will soon be opened by my passion, and the everlasting inheritance will be given to the elect. [[1:15|Repent|Pœnitemini]], that is, be pricked at heart and grieve for your sins, [[1:15|and believe the gospel|et credite Evangelio]], that is, the preaching and law of the Gospel which I set before you.

paras.t: Et præteriens Jesus secus mare Galilææ, vidit Simonem et Andream fratrem ejus. Hoc loco describit Evangelista vocationem quatuor Apostolorum ad Christi discipulatum, videlicet Petri et Andreæ, Jacobi et Joannis; patetque sententia ex his quæ in Matthæo prehabita sunt. Hic tamen additur unum verbum quod ibi non ponitur, utpote: cum mercenariis. Et est sensus, quod Jacobus et Joannes reliquerunt patrem suum Zebedæum et mercenarios, id est eos qui pro mercede eum juvabant in opere piscationis.
paras.en: [[1:16|And passing by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew his brother|Et præteriens Jesus secus mare Galilææ, vidit Simonem et Andream fratrem ejus]]. Here the Evangelist describes the calling of four Apostles to be Christ's disciples, namely Peter and Andrew, James and John; and the sense is plain from what was said before on Matthew[[Matt 4:18||]]. Here, however, one word is added that is not given there, namely: [[1:20|with his hired men|cum mercenariis]]. And the sense is that James and John left their father Zebedee and the hired men, that is, those who helped him for wages in the work of fishing.

paras.t: Et ingrediuntur Jesus ejusque discipuli Capharnaum, urbem in Galilæa præcipuam, in qua Christus ad tempus habitavit, et in principio suæ prædicationis multoties docuit, signaque fecit. Et statim sabbatis, id est die sabbati, quo Judæi maxime concurrebant ad audiendam lectionem legis et Prophetarum, ingressus in synagogam, id est domum in qua Judæi ad orandum et audiendum verbum Dei confluebant. Loquitur autem de synagoga in Capharnaum consistente. Docebat eos, id est Judæos concurrentes. Et stupebant, id est, multum mirabantur, super doctrina ejus. Cujus subjungitur ratio: erat enim docens eos quasi potestatem habens, hoc est, valde potenter et efficaciter loquens, corda audientium compungens et excitans, quasi ignea proferens verba, suamque prædicationem confirmans miraculis; et non sicut Scribæ, qui docebant, et non operabantur, habentes folia sine fructibus, foris perstrepentes, et intus parum aut nihil proficientes.
paras.en: [[1:21|And they entered into Capharnaum|Et ingrediuntur Capharnaum]], Jesus and his disciples, a chief city of Galilee, in which Christ lived for a time and at the beginning of his preaching often taught and worked signs. [[1:21|and forthwith upon the sabbath days|Et statim sabbatis]], that is, on the sabbath day, when the Jews most of all flocked together to hear the reading of the law and the Prophets, [[1:21|going into the synagogue|ingressus in synagogam]], that is, the house in which the Jews gathered to pray and to hear the word of God; he is speaking of the synagogue in Capharnaum. [[1:21|he taught them|Docebat eos]], that is, the Jews who flocked there. [[1:22|And they were astonished at his doctrine|Et stupebant super doctrina ejus]], that is, they wondered greatly. The reason is added: [[1:22|For he was teaching them as one having power|erat enim docens eos quasi potestatem habens]], that is, speaking very powerfully and effectively, piercing and stirring the hearts of his hearers, uttering as it were fiery words, and confirming his preaching with miracles; [[1:22|and not as the scribes|et non sicut Scribæ]], who taught and did not do, having leaves without fruit, noisy outside and profiting little or nothing within.

paras.t: Et erat in synagoga eorum homo in spiritu immundo, id est possessus a dæmone, Et clamavit dæmon per os hominis a se obsessi. Doluit enim de salutari doctrina Christi, et se expellendum expavit. Dicens: Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu Nazarene? id est, cur accessisti ad nos, qui tecum communionem nullam habemus, neque ad te pertinemus? Venisti perdere, id est vincere nos, nostram potestatem frangendo, et peccatores salvando, nosque expellendo atque ad inferos retrudendo? Scio quia sis Sanctus Dei, id est Sanctus Sanctorum, et Christus in lege promissus, per excellentiam Sanctus vocatus: de quo Daniel, Ungatur (inquit) Sanctus Sanctorum; et in Psalmo, Non dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem. Denique, quomodo dæmones et Judæi noverant Jesum esse Christum, an scilicet certitudinaliter, an conjecturaliter, sæpe tractatum est in Matthæo. Non enim dæmones hoc sciebant certitudine absoluta ac stabili, quemadmodum nec Judæi. Poterant tamen diaboli hoc certius agnovisse quam homines; imo et certitudinaliter hoc scivissent, nisi divina dispensatione fuissent prohibiti, ut Christi passio impleretur.
paras.en: [[1:23|And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit|Et erat in synagoga eorum homo in spiritu immundo]], that is, possessed by a demon; [[1:23|and he cried out|Et clamavit]], the demon, through the mouth of the man he possessed. For he grieved at Christ's saving teaching and was terrified of being cast out. [[1:24|Saying: What have we to do with thee, Jesus of Nazareth?|Dicens: Quid nobis et tibi, Jesu Nazarene?]] that is, why have you come to us, who have no fellowship with you and do not belong to you? [[1:24|Art thou come to destroy us?|venisti perdere nos?]], that is, to overcome us, breaking our power, saving sinners, and casting us out and thrusting us back into hell? [[1:24|I know who thou art, the Holy One of God|Scio quia sis Sanctus Dei]], that is, the Holy of Holies, and the Christ promised in the law, called the Holy One by excellence: of whom Daniel says, [[Dan 9:24|the Saint of saints may be anointed|Ungatur (inquit) Sanctus Sanctorum]]; and the Psalm, [[Ps 15:10|nor wilt thou give thy holy one to see corruption|Non dabis Sanctum tuum videre corruptionem]]. How the demons and the Jews knew that Jesus was the Christ, whether with certainty or by conjecture, has often been treated in Matthew. For the demons did not know it with absolute and stable certainty, as neither did the Jews. Yet the devils could have recognized it more certainly than men; indeed they would have known it with certainty had they not been prevented by divine dispensation, so that Christ's passion might be accomplished.

paras.t: Et comminatus est ei Jesus, dicens: Obmutesce, hoc est, ne amplius perhibeas testimonium mihi. Quum enim sim veritas, testimonio tuo non egeo, quum sis mendax, et vera prava intentione proferas, ut falsa miscendo decipias. Et exi ab homine isto. Et discerpens, id est, corporaliter affligens, eum spiritus immundus. Unde in Luca legitur, quod projecit eum in medium: nam invitus exivit. Et exclamans voce magna, quasi victus et violentiam passus tristissimusque effectus, exiit ab eo. Et mirati sunt omnes qui aderant, non solum in opere miraculoso, sed et in modo operis; ita ut conquirerent, id est, simul inter se quærerent, inter se dicentes: Quidnam est hoc? Non enim viderant simile fieri ab exorcistis Judæorum. Quænam doctrina hæc nova, id est prius inaudita, et documentis legis ac Prophetarum perfectior, quæ confirmatur prodigiis tam imperiosis? quia in potestate, id est magna et propria auctoritate, seu verbo imperiali, non adjuratorio, spiritibus immundis imperat, et obediunt ei. Videntur isti plurale ponere pro singulari. Non enim viderunt nisi unum obsessum sanari; sed eadem virtute qua videbant unum a Jesu sanatum, credebant et alios posse ab eo sanari. Et processit rumor, id est fama, ejus statim in omnem regionem Galilææ.
paras.en: [[1:25|And Jesus threatened him, saying: Speak no more|Et comminatus est ei Jesus, dicens: Obmutesce]], that is, bear witness to me no longer. For since I am the truth[[John 14:6||]], I do not need your testimony, since you are a liar, and utter true things with a wicked intention, to deceive by mixing in falsehoods. [[1:25|and go out of the man|Et exi ab homine isto]]. [[1:26|And the unclean spirit, tearing him|Et discerpens eum spiritus immundus]], that is, afflicting him bodily. Hence we read in Luke that [[Luke 4:35|the devil had thrown him into the midst|projecit eum in medium]]: for he went out unwillingly. [[1:26|and crying out with a loud voice|Et exclamans voce magna]], as one overcome and suffering violence and made most sorrowful, [[1:26|went out of him|exiit ab eo]]. [[1:27|And they were all amazed|Et mirati sunt omnes]] who were present, not only at the miraculous work but at the manner of the work, [[1:27|insomuch that they questioned among themselves, saying: What thing is this?|ita ut conquirerent inter se dicentes: Quidnam est hoc?]] For they had not seen the like done by the exorcists of the Jews. [[1:27|What is this new doctrine?|Quænam doctrina hæc nova]], that is, unheard of before, and more perfect than the teachings of the law and the Prophets, which is confirmed by such commanding wonders? [[1:27|For with power he commandeth even the unclean spirits: and they obey him|quia in potestate etiam spiritibus immundis imperat, et obediunt ei]], 'with power', that is, with great authority of his own, or with a word of command, not of adjuration. These men seem to put the plural for the singular: for they had seen only one possessed man healed; but by the same power by which they saw one healed by Jesus, they believed that others too could be healed by him. [[1:28|And the fame of him was spread forthwith into all the country of Galilee|Et processit rumor, id est fama, ejus statim in omnem regionem Galilææ]].

paras.t: Et protinus egredientes Jesus et ejus discipuli de synagoga, venerunt in domum Simonis et Andreæ cum Jacobo et Joanne. Intravit enim Jesus ad suos familiares amicos et notos, ad pausandum et reficiendum. Decumbebat autem, id est jacebat, socrus Simonis, id est mater conjugis Petri, febricitans. Et statim dicunt ei, id est, Christum rogabant, de illa, id est pro curatione ipsius. Et accedens elevavit eam, apprehensa manu ejus. Et continuo dimisit eam febris, id est, subito curata est, et ministrabat eis. De isto miraculo dicta sunt plura in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[1:29|And immediately going out of the synagogue|Et protinus egredientes de synagoga]], Jesus and his disciples, [[1:29|they came into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John|venerunt in domum Simonis et Andreæ cum Jacobo et Joanne]]. For Jesus went in to his intimate friends and acquaintances, to rest and refresh himself. [[1:30|And Simon's wife's mother lay in a fit of a fever|Decumbebat autem … socrus Simonis … febricitans]], 'lay', that is, was lying down; Simon's wife's mother, that is, the mother of Peter's wife. [[1:30|and forthwith they tell him of her|et statim dicunt ei de illa]], that is, they asked Christ for her healing. [[1:31|And coming to her, he lifted her up, taking her by the hand; and immediately the fever left her|Et accedens elevavit eam, apprehensa manu ejus. Et continuo dimisit eam febris]], that is, she was suddenly healed, [[1:31|and she ministered unto them|et ministrabat eis]]. More was said of this miracle in Matthew[[Matt 8:14||]].

paras.t: Vespere autem facto, scilicet, quum occidisset sol, afferebant ad eum omnes male habentes, id est infirmos loci illius. Audita enim curatione dæmoniaci et socrus Petri, conceperunt fiduciam, quod Christus ceteros omnes infirmos sanare posset ac dignaretur. Et erat omnis civitas congregata ad januam domus in qua exstitit Jesus, id est multi de civitate, juxta communem modum loquendi. Diversi enim ex diversis causis confluxerunt: quidam ex curiositate, propter novitatem gestorum; quidam ex necessitate; quidam, ut pro suis infirmis rogarent; quidam, ut tantorum signorum operationem viderent, vel ejus doctrinam audirent. Et curavit multos qui vexabantur variis languoribus. In Matthæo habetur, quod omnes infirmos adductos curaverit. Unde sensus est: Et curavit multos, id est omnes sibi oblatos, qui fuerant multi. Et dæmonia multa ejiciebat ab obsessis, solo verbo seu imperio; et non sinebat ea loqui, id est, non permisit dæmones dicere, quoniam sciebant eum, hoc est, quod noscerent Jesum esse Christum, secundum modum notitiæ jam expressæ. Eisdem autem rationibus prohibuit hoc istis dæmonibus, quibus et dæmoni de quo paulo ante facta est mentio.
paras.en: [[1:32|And when it was evening, after sunset|Vespere autem facto, scilicet, quum occidisset sol]], [[1:32|they brought to him all that were ill|afferebant ad eum omnes male habentes]], that is, the sick of that place [the printed text adds in brackets 'and that were possessed with devils']. For having heard of the healing of the possessed man and of Peter's mother-in-law, they conceived confidence that Christ could and would deign to heal all the other sick. [[1:33|And all the city was gathered together at the door|Et erat omnis civitas congregata ad januam]] of the house in which Jesus was, that is, many of the city, in the common manner of speaking. For different people flocked together for different reasons: some out of curiosity, because of the novelty of the deeds; some out of necessity; some to pray for their sick; some to see such great signs worked, or to hear his teaching. [[1:34|And he healed many that were troubled with divers diseases|Et curavit multos qui vexabantur variis languoribus]]. In Matthew we have it that he healed all the sick who were brought[[Matt 8:16||]]. So the sense is: and he healed many, that is, all who were brought to him, who had been many. [[1:34|And he cast out many devils|Et dæmonia multa ejiciebat]] from the possessed, by his word or command alone; [[1:34|and he suffered them not to speak, because they knew him|et non sinebat ea loqui, quoniam sciebant eum]], that is, he did not allow the demons to say that they knew Jesus to be the Christ, in the manner of knowledge already explained. And he forbade it to these demons for the same reasons as to the demon mentioned a little before[[1:25||]].

paras.t: Et diluculo valde surgens, contra eos qui diu dormiunt: justus enim cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum; egressus de civitate, abiit in desertum locum, docens post perpetrationem miraculorum et sermocinationes præclaras, fugere laudes humanas hominumque adspectum; ibique orabat, ad designandum quod locus solitarius aptissimus est ad orandum, quamvis ipse nullo exteriori poterat ab unione interna cum Deo impediri, sicut nec aliquo modo poterat adjuvari. Unde, quod gratia orationis toties solitudinem petiit, pro nostra utique fecit instructione, ut et nos ita agamus. Et prosecutus, id est prope secutus est eum Simon, et qui cum eo erant, id est discipuli alii: decuit namque ut magistrum mente et corpore sequerentur. Et quum invenissent eum in loco orationis, in quo se paululum elongavit ab eis, orans Patrem suum in abscondito, dixerunt ei: Quia omnes, de quibus jam dictum est, quærunt te animarum et corporum incomparabilem medicum et efficacissimum sanatorem. Nempe, ut dictum est, ob diversas causas quærebant et concurrebant ad eum.
paras.en: [[1:35|And rising very early|Et diluculo valde surgens]], against those who sleep long: for the just man [[Ecclus 39:6|will give his heart to resort early to the Lord|cor suum tradet ad vigilandum diluculo ad Dominum]]; [[1:35|going out|egressus]] of the city, [[1:35|he went into a desert place|abiit in desertum locum]], teaching us, after working miracles and giving splendid discourses, to flee human praise and the gaze of men; [[1:35|and there he prayed|ibique orabat]], to show that a solitary place is best suited to prayer; though he himself could not be hindered by anything outward from his inward union with God, as neither could he be helped in any way. So his seeking solitude so often for the sake of prayer he did for our instruction, that we too may do so. [[1:36|And Simon and they that were with him followed after him|Et prosecutus est eum Simon, et qui cum eo erant]], 'followed after', that is, followed close; 'they that were with him', that is, the other disciples: for it was fitting that they should follow their master in mind and body. [[1:37|And when they had found him|Et quum invenissent eum]] in the place of prayer, where he had withdrawn a little from them, praying to his Father in secret[[Matt 6:6||]], [[1:37|they said to him: All seek for thee|dixerunt ei: Quia omnes quærunt te]], all those spoken of already, seeking you as the incomparable physician of souls and bodies and the most effective healer. For, as has been said, they sought him and flocked to him for different reasons.

paras.t: Et ait illis: Eamus in proximos vicos et civitates, eundo de distanti in distans per media, et de loco ad locum ordinate, ut et ibi prædicem: ad hoc enim veni per incarnationem in mundum, videlicet, ut omnibus ovibus perditis domus Israel sine personarum acceptione, verbum salutis proponam. Et erat prædicans in synagogis eorum, hoc est proximarum civitatum, et in omni Galilæa, et dæmonia ejiciens.
paras.en: [[1:38|And he saith to them: Let us go into the neighbouring towns and cities|Et ait illis: Eamus in proximos vicos et civitates]], going from one distant place to another through those between, and from place to place in order, [[1:38|that I may preach there also|ut et ibi prædicem]]: [[1:38|for to this purpose am I come|ad hoc enim veni]] into the world by the incarnation, namely to set the word of salvation before all the lost sheep of the house of Israel[[Matt 15:24||]] without respect of persons. [[1:39|And he was preaching in their synagogues|Et erat prædicans in synagogis eorum]], that is, of the neighbouring cities, [[1:39|and in all Galilee and casting out devils|et in omni Galilæa, et dæmonia ejiciens]].

paras.t: Consequenter in speciali describitur curatio unius leprosi propter magnitudinem devotionis suæ ac fidei. Devotio enim et fides leprosi ostendebantur in hoc, quod genu flexo dixit ad Jesum: Si vis, potes me mundare. Porro miraculum istud et expositio ejus, descripta sunt supra in Matthæo. Aliquid tamen hic additur, scilicet: At ille, id est leprosus a Christo curatus, cui præceperat Christus ut nemini diceret gratiam sanitatis sibi collatæ, egressus a Christo, cœpit prædicare et diffamare, hoc est diversimode promulgare, sermonem, id est narrationem de sua curatione. Non tamen inobediens fuit, quia ex dilectione et devotione Christi hoc fecit. Christi autem præceptum intelligendum erat, ne ex vanitate et sine ratione ad jactantiam faceret hoc. Vel, secundum alios, Christus præcepit ut taceret, usque dum ostendisset se sacerdoti, et postea dicere potuit. Ita ut jam non, hoc est vix vel difficulter, posset Jesus manifeste in civitatem introire, propter multitudinem sibi occurrentem et eum comprimentem vicissim, sed foris in desertis locis esse. Poterat tamen Christus omnia, secundum suam absolutam potentiam; sed Evangelista loquitur secundum exteriorem apparentiam et solitum modum loquendi. Et conveniebant ad eum undique, diversis ex causis, ut dixi.
paras.en: Next is described in particular the healing of one leper, because of the greatness of his devotion and faith. For the leper's devotion and faith were shown in that, [[1:40|kneeling down, said to him: If thou wilt thou canst make me clean|genu flexo dixit ad Jesum: Si vis, potes me mundare]], to Jesus. This miracle and its exposition have been written above on Matthew[[Matt 8:2||]]. Something, however, is added here, namely: [[1:45|But he being gone out|At ille egressus]], that is, the leper healed by Christ, whom Christ had commanded to tell no one of the grace of health bestowed on him, going out from Christ, [[1:45|began to publish and to blaze abroad the word|cœpit prædicare, et diffamare sermonem]], that is, to spread abroad in various ways the account of his healing. Yet he was not disobedient, since he did this out of love and devotion to Christ; and Christ's command was to be understood as forbidding him to do it out of vanity and without reason, for boasting. Or, according to others, Christ commanded him to be silent until he had shown himself to the priest, and afterwards he could speak. [[1:45|so that he could not openly go into the city|Ita ut jam non, hoc est vix vel difficulter, posset Jesus manifeste in civitatem introire]], 'could not', that is, hardly or with difficulty, because of the multitude running to meet him and pressing on him in turn, [[1:45|but was without in desert places|sed foris in desertis locis esse]]. Christ could, however, do all things by his absolute power; but the Evangelist speaks according to the outward appearance and the usual manner of speaking. [[1:45|And they flocked to him from all sides|Et conveniebant ad eum undique]], for different reasons, as I have said.

2.title: Elucidatio capituli secundi: Et iterum intravit Capharnaum post dies octo
2.title_en: Explanation of the second chapter: “And again he entered into Capharnaum after eight days”

paras.t: Et iterum intravit Jesus Capharnaum post dies octo; [et auditum est quod in domo esset;] et convenerunt multi, ita ut non caperet, hoc est, contineri et capi seu stare non possent, neque ad januam domus in qua exstitit Christus. Sed aliqui ipsam domum introierunt. Et loquebatur eis verbum vitæ æternæ.
paras.en: [[2:1|And again he entered into Capharnaum|Et iterum intravit Jesus Capharnaum]] after eight days [Denis's text reads post dies octo, “after eight days”; the Vulgate has post dies, “after some days”]; [[2:2|and it was heard that he was in the house|et auditum est quod in domo esset]] [these words are supplied by the editors in brackets]; [[2:2|And many came together, so that there was no room|et convenerunt multi, ita ut non caperet]], that is, they could not be contained and held or find standing room, [[2:2|no, not even at the door|neque ad januam]] of the house in which Christ was. But some went into the house itself. [[2:2|And he spoke to them the word|Et loquebatur eis verbum]] of eternal life.

paras.t: Consequenter describitur curatio paralytici. De qua plenius dictum est in evangelio S. Matthæi: idcirco nunc celerius pertransibo. Et venerunt viri aliqui ferentes ad eum, hoc est ad Jesum, paralyticum, qui a quatuor portabatur una cum lecto in quo jacuit. Et quum non possent offerre, id est præsentare eum paralyticum illi, scilicet Christo, præ turba: quoniam propter turbam non poterant per januam ingredi domum in qua docuit Christus; nudaverunt tectum ubi erat, id est, tectum domus illius ascenderunt, et, facta illic apertura, per tegulas deposuerunt lectum cum languido. Unde nunc subditur: et patefacientes, id est, tectum illud aperientes, submiserunt grabatum in quo paralyticus jacebat. Tecta enim in locis illis plana fuerunt, habueruntque januam qua ad ea ascendebatur: per quam aliqui dicunt lectum fuisse submissum cum paralytico isto. Quia tamen hic dicitur quod nudaverunt tectum, et Lucas quoque ait quod per tegulas submiserunt infirmum, magis apparet quod in ipso tecto novam fecerunt aperturam.
paras.en: Next is described the healing of the paralytic, of which more has been said in the Gospel of St Matthew[[Matt 9:2||]] [the margin as read gives Matth. x, 2-7; the healing of the paralytic is Matt 9:2-7]; therefore I shall now pass over it more quickly. [[2:3|And they came|Et venerunt]], some men, [[2:3|to him, bringing|ferentes ad eum]], that is, to Jesus, [[2:3|one sick of the palsy, who was carried by four|paralyticum, qui a quatuor portabatur]], together with the bed on which he lay. [[2:4|And when they could not offer him|Et quum non possent offerre]], that is, present the paralytic to him, namely to Christ, [[2:4|for the multitude|præ turba]], since because of the crowd they could not enter by the door the house in which Christ was teaching, [[2:4|they uncovered the roof where he was|nudaverunt tectum ubi erat]], that is, they climbed onto the roof of that house and, making an opening there, let the bed down with the sick man through the tiles. So it is now added: [[2:4|and opening it|et patefacientes]], that is, opening that roof, [[2:4|they let down the bed wherein the man sick of the palsy lay|submiserunt grabatum in quo paralyticus jacebat]]. For the roofs in those parts were flat, and had a door by which one went up to them; and some say that the bed was let down with this paralytic through that door. But since it is said here that they uncovered the roof, and Luke too says that they let the sick man down [[Luke 5:19|through the tiles|per tegulas]], it seems more likely that they made a new opening in the roof itself.

paras.t: Cetera quæ hic de isto miraculo recitantur, patent ex his quæ in Matthæo dicta sunt. Hic tamen dicitur, quod Jesus cognovit spiritu suo cogitationes Scribarum. Et potest per spiritum Christi intelligi Spiritus Sanctus, de quo ait Apostolus: Si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est ejus. Cujus utique Spiritus virtute et gratia, Christus ut homo agnovit cogitationes universorum. Et potest quoque per spiritum Christi intelligi intellectus animæ ejus, quo omnia præterita, præsentia et futura cognoscit.
paras.en: The rest of what is related here of this miracle is plain from what was said on Matthew. Here, however, it is said that Jesus knew [[2:8|in his spirit|spiritu suo]] the thoughts of the Scribes. And by the spirit of Christ may be understood the Holy Ghost, of whom the Apostle says: [[Rom 8:9|if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his|Si quis Spiritum Christi non habet, hic non est ejus]]. By the power and grace of this Spirit, Christ as man knew the thoughts of all. And by the spirit of Christ may also be understood the intellect of His soul, by which He knows all things past, present and to come.

paras.t: Et egressus est rursus ad mare quod currit per Galilæam. Judæi autem quamlibet magnam congregationem aquarum nominant mare: quem loquendi modum servaverunt Evangelistæ. Et quum præteriret loca illa, vidit Levi Alphæi, id est Matthæum filium Alphæi: Matthæus enim alio nomine dictus est Levi; sedentem ad telonium. Porro, quæ subjunguntur hoc loco de vocatione Matthæi et punctis annexis, dicta atque exposita sunt in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[2:13|And he went forth again to the sea side|Et egressus est rursus ad mare]], the sea that runs through Galilee. For the Jews call any large gathering of waters a sea, and the Evangelists kept this manner of speaking. [[2:14|And when he was passing by|Et quum præteriret]] those parts, [[2:14|he saw Levi, the son of Alpheus|vidit Levi Alphæi]], that is, Matthew the son of Alpheus, for Matthew was also called by another name, Levi, [[2:14|sitting at the receipt of custom|sedentem ad telonium]]. What is added here about the calling of Matthew and the points connected with it has been said and explained on Matthew[[Matt 9:9||]] [the margin as read gives Matth. x, 9-13; the calling of Matthew is Matt 9:9-13].

paras.t: Deinceps Marcus describit disceptationem discipulorum Joannis et Pharisæorum cum Jesu; et littera patet plenissime ex his quæ in Matthæo dicta sunt.
paras.en: Next Mark describes the dispute of the disciples of John and of the Pharisees with Jesus; and the letter is entirely plain from what was said on Matthew[[Matt 9:14||]].

paras.t: Et factum est iterum quum sabbatis ambularet Jesus per sata. Hic Evangelista commemorat quomodo Jesu ambulante per agros seminatos et blada portantes, discipuli ejus fame compulsi, spicas sumpserunt et comederunt: quo viso Pharisæi increpabant Christum. Quidquid autem hic scribitur de hoc facto, supra expositum est in Matthæo. Sed quærendum est, quomodo Marcus dicat ipsum David intrasse domum Dei sub Abiathar principe sacerdotum, quum in libris Regum legatur id factum sub Achimelech pontifice? Et respondendum, quod iste Abiathar fuit filius Achimelech, succedens ei in sacerdotii principatu; et patre ejus vivente, egit interdum vices ipsius: ideo David dicitur introisse domum Dei sub eo.
paras.en: [[2:23|And it came to pass again, as the Lord walked through the corn fields on the sabbath|Et factum est iterum quum sabbatis ambularet Jesus per sata]]. Here the Evangelist records how, as Jesus walked through fields that were sown and bearing grain, His disciples, driven by hunger, took ears of corn and ate them; seeing which, the Pharisees rebuked Christ. Whatever is written here of this deed has been explained above on Matthew[[Matt 12:1||]]. But it must be asked how Mark can say that David himself [[2:26|went into the house of God, under Abiathar the high priest|intrasse domum Dei sub Abiathar principe sacerdotum]], when in the books of Kings we read that it was done under the high priest Achimelech[[1 Kings 21:1||]]. And the answer is that this Abiathar was the son of Achimelech, who succeeded him in the chief priesthood; and while his father was still living he sometimes acted in his place: so David is said to have entered the house of God under him.

3.title: Expositio capituli tertii: Et introivit iterum in synagogam
3.title_en: Exposition of the third chapter: “And he entered again into the synagogue”

paras.t: Deinde recitat Evangelista quomodo Christus sanaverit hominem cujus aruit manus. Et planus est sensus hujus loci ex his quæ in Matthæo dicta sunt. Et circumspiciens Jesus eos, id est incredulos Judæos ac Pharisæos, cum ira per zelum, id est cum moderato appetitu vindictæ propter injuriam Deo illatam, vel saltem cum vultu iram prætendente. Fuit autem in Christo ira per zelum: quæ tamen actum rationis in ipso nullatenus perturbabat, quia in ipso unaquæque potentia animæ exercuit actum suum, non impediendo alterius actum potentiæ. In aliis tamen ira, etiam quæ est per zelum, turbat aliqualiter oculum mentis, quoniam anima circa actum unius potentiæ multum intenta et occupata, impeditur in actu alterius potentiæ. Hæc autem ira mansuetudini non repugnat, cujus est passionem iræ ordinare; sed ira per vitium. Contristatus super cæcitate cordis eorum, misericorditer condolens eis. Fuit ergo in Christo tristitia virtuosa ex caritate et pietate descendens, quia errantibus compatiebatur. Fuit quoque in eo passio tristitiæ moderata ac naturalis, quia inferior pars animæ ejus sequebatur partem superiorem. Quod autem in Isaia de Christo inducitur, Non erit tristis nec turbulentus, intelligendum est de sæculari, carnali et inordinata tristitia, quæ non cadit in virum perfectum, quemadmodum Salomon contestatur: Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist relates how Christ healed the man whose hand was withered; and the sense of this passage is plain from what was said on Matthew[[Matt 12:10||]] [the margin prints Matth. xi, 10-13; the healing of the withered hand is Matt 12:10-13]. [[3:5|And looking round about on them|Et circumspiciens eos]], that is, on the unbelieving Jews and Pharisees, [[3:5|with anger|cum ira]], an anger of zeal, that is, with a measured desire to punish the injury done to God, or at least with a countenance that showed anger. There was in Christ the anger of zeal [ira per zelum: anger roused by zeal for what is right, as distinct from ira per vitium, the sinful anger of vice], which nevertheless in no way disturbed the act of reason in Him, because in Him each power of the soul exercised its own act without hindering the act of another power. In others, however, anger, even the anger of zeal, somewhat clouds the eye of the mind, because the soul, much intent upon and occupied with the act of one power, is hindered in the act of another. This anger is not opposed to meekness, whose part is to order the passion of anger; what is opposed to it is the anger of vice. [[3:5|being grieved for the blindness of their hearts|contristatus super cæcitate cordis eorum]], mercifully grieving with them. So there was in Christ a virtuous sadness coming down from charity and pity, because He felt compassion for those who went astray. There was in Him also a moderate and natural passion of sadness, because the lower part of His soul followed the higher. And what is brought forward in Isaias concerning Christ, [[Is 42:4|He shall not be sad, nor troublesome|Non erit tristis, neque turbulentus]], is to be understood of worldly, carnal and disordered sadness, which does not befall a perfect man, as Solomon testifies: [[Prov 12:21|Whatsoever shall befall the just man, shall not make him sad|Non contristabit justum quidquid ei acciderit]].

paras.t: Exeuntes autem Pharisæi, cum Herodianis, id est militibus Herodis, vel, ut alii dicunt, cum his qui putabant Herodem esse Christum, consilium faciebant quomodo illum perderent, id est, qualiter Jesum occiderent.
paras.en: [[3:6|And the Pharisees going out|Exeuntes autem pharisæi]] [[3:6|made a consultation with the Herodians|cum Herodianis consilium faciebant]], that is, with Herod's soldiers, or, as others say, with those who thought that Herod was the Christ, [[3:6|how they might destroy him|quomodo eum perderent]], that is, how they might kill Jesus.

paras.t: Et Jesus cum discipulis suis secessit ad mare, dans locum furentibus. Et dixit discipulis suis ut navicula sibi deserviret, id est, navem sibi adducerent, eamque intraret, et staret in mari juxta ripam, propter turbam stantem et accurrentem in terra, ne comprimerent eum. In quo ostendit se vere fuisse passibilem, atque sæpe ad tempus vitasse incommoda corporis, ut tempore divinitus præstituto pateretur. Et quamvis poterat turbæ pressuram sine læsione et pœna sustinere per viam mirabilem, noluit tamen humanum subsidium devitare, ut veritatem assumptæ naturæ ostenderet. Multos enim sanabat, ita ut irruerent in eum ut illum tangerent. Nam virtus exibat de illo, sanabatque omnes.
paras.en: [[3:7|But Jesus retired with his disciples to the sea|Jesus autem cum discipulis suis secessit ad mare]], giving way to their fury. [[3:9|And he spoke to his disciples that a small ship should wait on him|Et dicit discipulis suis ut navicula sibi deserviret]]: that is, that they should bring a boat to Him, so that He might go into it and stand on the water near the shore, [[3:9|because of the multitude|propter turbam]] standing and running together on the land, [[3:9|lest they should throng him|ne comprimerent eum]]. In this He showed that He was truly able to suffer, and that He often avoided bodily hardships for a time, so that He might suffer at the time divinely appointed. And though He could have borne the pressing of the crowd without hurt or pain by a miraculous way, He would not refuse a human help, so as to show the reality of the nature He had taken. [[3:10|For he healed many, so that they pressed upon him for to touch him|multos enim sanabat, ita ut irruerent in eum ut illum tangerent]]. For [[Luke 6:19|virtue went out from him and healed all|virtus de illo exibat, et sanabat omnes]].

paras.t: Quotquot autem habebant plagas, id est varias infirmitates, et spiritus immundi, id est diaboli in obsessis; vel, Spiritus immundi, id est obsessi a dæmonibus; quum illum videbant, procidebant ei, sponte vel coacte reverentiam exhibendo: et si aliqui languidi talem infirmitatem habebant, quod ante suam curationem se coram Jesu prosternere non valebant, tamen sanitate recepta, hoc facere poterant. Et clamabant dæmones per obsessos, dicentes: Tu es Filius Dei. Hoc conjecturaliter asserebant, non cum certitudine constanti et absoluta. Et vehementer comminabatur eis ne manifestarent illum, id est, ne ultra dicerent coram populo Jesum esse Christum Filium Dei. Contempsit enim testimonium dæmonum, propter causas introductas. Sed cur dæmones dixerunt tot bona de Christo? Dicendum, quod coacte vel malo fine, et ob alias causas quas non est facile excogitare: et forte, ut ejus passionem impedirent, scientes quod nunquam crucifigerent Dominum gloriæ ipsi Judæi, si eum agnoscerent.
paras.en: [[3:10|as many as had evils|quotquot habebant plagas]], that is, various sicknesses, [[3:11|And the unclean spirits|Et spiritus immundi]], that is, the devils in the possessed; or, 'the unclean spirits', that is, those possessed by demons, [[3:11|when they saw him, fell down before him|cum illum videbant, procidebant ei]], showing reverence willingly or under compulsion. And if some of the sick had such an infirmity that they could not prostrate themselves before Jesus before they were cured, yet once their health was restored they could do so. [[3:11|and they cried, saying|et clamabant, dicentes]], the demons speaking through the possessed: [[3:12|Thou art the Son of God.|Tu es Filius Dei.]] This they asserted by conjecture, not with constant and absolute certainty. [[3:12|And he strictly charged them that they should not make him known.|Et vehementer comminabatur eis ne manifestarent illum.]] That is, that they should no longer say before the people that Jesus was the Christ, the Son of God; for He scorned the testimony of demons, for the reasons given earlier[[Mark 1:25||]]. But why did the demons say so many good things of Christ? It must be said: under compulsion, or with an evil purpose, and for other reasons not easy to work out; and perhaps to hinder His passion, knowing that the Jews themselves would never crucify the Lord of glory if they recognized Him[[1 Cor 2:8||]].

paras.t: Et ascendens Jesus in montem, vocavit ad se quos voluit ipse, id est quos præ aliis ad hoc elegit, videlicet quosdam ex discipulis; et venerunt ad eum in montem. Et fecit ut essent duodecim cum illo, id est, duodecim Apostolos fecit sibi specialiter adhærere, ut essent sibi quasi collaterales, familiares et proximi; et ut mitteret eos prædicare. Et imposuit Simoni nomen aliud, scilicet Petrus, quod interpretatur firmus, sive obediens principalis. Et Jacobum filium Zebedæi, et Joannem fratrem Jacobi vocavit, et imposuit eis nomina Boanerges, quod est, filii tonitrui, propter altisonam et efficacissimam prædicationem ipsorum, et quia in transfiguratione Christi audierunt, vel potius audituri erant vocem Patris dicentis: Hic est Filius meus dilectus. Hujuscemodi enim vox appellatur tonitruum, eo modo quo scriptum est in Job: Quis poterit tonitruum magnitudinis ejus intueri? Hæc autem mutatio nominum spiritualem innovationem et gratiam specialem designavit. Cetera quæ hic dicuntur, plenius elucidata sunt in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[3:13|And going up into a mountain, he called unto him whom he would himself|Et ascendens in montem vocavit ad se quos voluit ipse]], that is, those whom He chose for this before others, namely some of the disciples; [[3:13|and they came to him|et venerunt ad eum]] on the mountain. [[3:14|And he made that twelve should be with him|Et fecit ut essent duodecim cum illo]]: that is, He made twelve Apostles cleave to Him in a special way, to be, as it were, His companions at His side, His familiars and His nearest; [[3:14|and that he might send them to preach|et ut mitteret eos prædicare]]. [[3:16|And to Simon he gave the name|Et imposuit Simoni nomen]], a new one, namely Peter, which is interpreted 'firm', or 'obedient chief'. And He called [[3:17|James the son of Zebedee, and John the brother of James; and he named them Boanerges, which is, The sons of thunder|Jacobum Zebedæi, et Joannem fratrem Jacobi, et imposuit eis nomina Boanerges, quod est, Filii tonitrui]], because of their lofty-sounding and most effective preaching, and because at Christ's transfiguration they heard, or rather were to hear, the voice of the Father saying: [[Matt 17:5|This is my beloved Son|Hic est Filius meus dilectus]]. For such a voice is called thunder, in the way it is written in Job: [[Job 26:14|who shall be able to behold the thunder of his greatness|quis poterit tonitruum magnitudinis illius intueri]]? This change of names signified a spiritual renewal and a special grace. The rest of what is said here was more fully explained on Matthew[[Matt 10:1||]].

paras.t: Et veniunt ad domum. Et convenit iterum turba ad Jesum, ut salutis verbum audirent, ita ut non possent neque panem manducare, id est, tam ferventer ac perseveranter insistebat Christus verbo prædicationis, quod discipuli ejus non habebant quietum tempus ad manducandum. Et quum audissent sui, id est, quum discipuli Christi: et maxime quidam ex consanguineis suis ex parte Matris, de quibus ait Joannes, quod fratres ejus nondum credebant in eum: quum igitur isti audissent verba Jesu, quæ erant supernaturalia, ardua, insolita, rudibusque Judæis penitus inaudita, exierunt tenere eum, hoc est comprehendere vel ligare Jesum tanquam arrepticium vel insanum. Dicebant enim: Quoniam in furorem versus est, id est furiosus effectus. Quoniam enim audierunt eum talia prædicare, nec a prædicatione cessare, nec corporalia commoda curare, opinati sunt quod esset in furorem conversus: quemadmodum Festus ait ad Paulum, Multæ litteræ ad insaniam te convertunt. Voluerunt ergo Jesum tenere, ne ex insania, sibi ipsi vel aliis nocumentum inferret. Et Scribæ qui ab Jerosolymis descenderant, dicebant: Quoniam Beelzebub habet, id est, dæmone sic vocato obsessus est, et quia in principe dæmoniorum ejicit dæmonia. Locus iste in Matthæo plene atque diffuse expositus est, ita ut illis pensatis, ista facillime intelligantur. Item quod subditur, Et veniunt Mater ejus et fratres, explanatum quoque est in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[3:20|And they come to a house, and the multitude cometh together again|Et veniunt ad domum: et convenit iterum turba]] to Jesus, to hear the word of salvation, [[3:20|so that they could not so much as eat bread|ita ut non possent neque panem manducare]]: that is, Christ kept at the word of preaching so fervently and so constantly that His disciples had no quiet time to eat. [[3:21|And when his friends had heard of it|Et cum audissent sui]]: that is, Christ's disciples, and especially certain of His kinsmen on His Mother's side, of whom John says that [[John 7:5|neither did his brethren believe in him|neque enim fratres ejus credebant in eum]]; when these, then, had heard the words of Jesus, which were supernatural, lofty, unaccustomed and wholly unheard-of to the unlettered Jews, [[3:21|they went out to lay hold on him|exierunt tenere eum]], that is, to seize or bind Jesus as one possessed or insane. [[3:21|For they said: He is become mad.|dicebant enim: Quoniam in furorem versus est.]] That is, He has become raving. For since they heard Him preaching such things, never ceasing from preaching, and taking no care for bodily comforts, they supposed He had turned to madness, as Festus said to Paul: [[Acts 26:24|much learning doth make thee mad|multæ te litteræ ad insaniam convertunt]]. So they wanted to hold Jesus, lest in His madness He should do harm to Himself or to others. [[3:22|And the scribes who were come down from Jerusalem, said: He hath Beelzebub|Et scribæ, qui ab Jerosolymis descenderant, dicebant: Quoniam Beelzebub habet]], that is, He is possessed by the demon so called, [[3:22|and by the prince of devils he casteth out devils|et quia in principe dæmoniorum ejicit dæmonia]]. This passage was expounded fully and at length on Matthew[[Matt 12:24||]], so that once that is weighed, this is very easily understood. Likewise what follows, [[3:31|And his mother and his brethren came|Et veniunt mater ejus et fratres]], was also explained on Matthew[[Matt 12:46||]].
